hints.title: 1 · Reproduce two stale clients
hints.body: Send two requests with expected_version 0. The first commits; the second must not overwrite it.

hints.title: 2 · Move the guard into the database
hints.body: A Ruby comparison followed by an unconditional write races. Use a conditional SQL update or a correctly scoped row lock.

hints.title: 3 · Include the audit in the transaction
hints.body: A failed audit must roll back the amount and revision. Database uniqueness protects the history even when model validation is bypassed.

criteria.title: Lost-update protection
criteria.target: The database guards the expected revision and increments exactly once.
criteria.probe: Why is checking version in Ruby before update insufficient?
criteria.practice: Trace two interleaved updates through SQL predicates.

criteria.title: Atomic audit history
criteria.target: The committed amount and immutable amendment agree, with rollback on storage failures.
criteria.probe: When must the old amount be read to keep audit evidence accurate?
criteria.practice: Inject failure after the conditional update.

criteria.title: Database integrity
criteria.target: A unique amendment revision and positive invoice amount survive validation bypass.
criteria.practice: Use insert_all and update_columns to bypass models.

criteria.title: Client and tenant contracts
criteria.target: Strict input and scoped identity preserve clients while reporting conflicts.
criteria.probe: How would an If-Match contract differ from this body version?
criteria.practice: Design a client conflict-resolution flow with a fresh read.

follow_up: Add line-item editing and total recalculation. Decide whether one invoice revision guards every line item and how clients resolve conflicting changes.
